Setup times range from minutes to hours for smaller systems, to hours or days for larger systems. Midsize to large systems can be transported in 20-ft and 40-ft standard shipping containers. These systems do not require permanent foundations and instead use custom trailers or shipping containers in combination with outriggers and anchors to provide safety and stability in all wind conditions (Summerville at al. 2022). These deployable wind systems are often paired with solar and battery energy storage to form a microgrid, offering reliable, on-site power for communications, water filtration, heat, lights, and medical equipment. Power systems powered by wind and solar energy help reduce reliance on liquid fuels for diesel generators that must be regularly delivered to the facility (McDermott- Murphy 2022). Deployable wind energy systems are currently being developed by U.S.-headquartered companies, such as a 12-kW portable wind turbine by Uprise Energy and the 30-kW Deployable Advanced Renewable Power System by Bergey Windpower Company (Uprise Energy n.d.; Bergey Windpower Company n.d.-a). Bergey Windpower offers a 10-kW wind turbine with a height of 23 feet that is capable of being connected to the grid and is certified by the Small Wind Certification Council (Bergey Windpower Company n.d.-b). Global competitors offer a range of commercialized options. Canadian-based Aurea Technologies markets the 40-W Shine Turbine system, which operates within an 8- to 28-mile- per-hour wind speed range and can be packed in a backpack (Shine Turbine 2025). E.7 Tactical Hydrogen Hydrogen generators can provide tactical point-of-need energy and are already being tested for DOW applications. Hydrogen can serve as an alternative to diesel generators, serving as self- sufficient power sources and reducing concerns related to diesel resupply as well as detectability (e.g., reducing heat, smoke, and noise) (Espinosa 2025; Kauffman 2025; Pasquini 2025). Multiple innovations and demonstration projects reflect progress towards tactical hydrogen systems for military applications. • A Hydrogen at the Tactical Edge of Contested Logistics (HyTEC) system is an electrolysis-based system using electricity from other sources to produce point-of-use hydrogen for expeditionary applications including small generators and unmanned aviation equipment (DIU 2025). As of 2025, this system is being tested at Marine Corps Base Hawaii and Marine Corps Air Station Yuma. • A portable Hydrogen Small Unit Power (H-SUP) system prototype has been developed by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory to function as a fuel cell electric generator able to support remote field operations where low detectability is critical (Pasquini 2025).
